sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

- When asked about: extensions (docs/extensions.md, examples/extensions/), themes (docs/themes.md), skills (docs/skills.md), prompt templates (docs/prompt-templates.md), TUI components (docs/tui.md), keybindings (docs/keybindings.md), SDK integrations (docs/sdk.md), custom providers (docs/custom-provider.md), adding models (docs/models.md), pi packages (docs/packages.md), environment variables (docs/environment-variables.md), MCP servers (docs/mcp.md), codemode scripts and non-LLM models such as classifiers and image models (docs/codemode.md)
- When working on pi topics, read the docs and examples, and follow .md cross-references before implementing
- Always read pi .md files completely and follow links to related docs (e.g., tui.md for TUI API details)
</docs>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: mcp__blender__get_python_api_docs
toolsAdded.description:
Return the Blender Python API docs for *identifier*, or list
modules matching a trailing-``*`` discovery pattern.

*identifier* should be a fully-qualified Python name (e.g.
``bpy.app`` or ``bpy.types.Scene.frame_current``).
The trailing-``*`` forms are supported as discovery entry-points:

- ``*`` enumerates the top-level modules (``bpy``, ``bmesh``,
  ``mathutils``, ``gpu``, ...).
- ``X.*`` enumerates the direct-child identifiers under the
  *X* namespace (``bpy.*`` -> ``bpy.app``, ``bpy.context``, ...).

Both return a ``namespace`` response even when ``X.rst`` would
otherwise resolve to ``exact``; the ``.*`` form lets an agent
force the child listing.

The response always carries ``kind``, ``found``, and ``identifier``.
The remaining keys depend on ``kind``:

- ``"exact"`` (``found=True``): ``<identifier>.rst`` was read.
  Extra keys: ``content`` (RST text), ``examples``. When the
  file exceeds 32 KB, ``content`` is replaced with a dot-point
  summary of the file's top-level definitions (prefixed by a
  header noting the truncation) and ``examples`` is empty -
  re-query individual members for their rendered blocks.
- ``"namespace"`` (``found=True``):
  no ``<identifier>.rst`` but ``<identifier>.<child>.rst`` siblings exist.
  Extra key: ``submodules`` (list of child identifiers).
- ``"definition"`` (``found=True``):
  *identifier* is defined inside a parent RST
  (e.g. ``bpy.props.IntProperty`` lives in ``bpy.props.rst``).
  Extra keys: ``content`` (rendered block), ``examples``.
- ``"partial"`` (``found=False``):
  the parent RST was located but the trailing component isn't defined in it.
  Extra keys:
  - ``parent`` the identifier whose RST was loaded.
  - ``available`` top-level definitions in that RST.
  - ``submodules`` sibling identifiers ``<parent>.<child>`` with their own RSTs,
    filtered to those whose last component contains every character of the missing tail.

  For a toctree landing page like ``bpy.types`` ``available`` is empty and ``submodules``
  is the near-miss list; for a self-contained module like ``bpy.props`` it's the reverse.
- ``"suggestions"`` (``found=False``):
  no direct match, but *identifier* appears as a component of other files.
  Extra key: ``suggestions`` (list of full identifiers).
- ``"missing"`` (``found=False``): nothing matched.

``examples`` (present on the ``exact`` and ``definition`` kinds)
is a list of ``{path, content}`` entries referenced from this documentation.

toolsAdded.name: mcp__blender__search_api_docs
toolsAdded.description:
Full-text search over the bundled Blender Python API reference.

Returns a ranked list of hits. Each hit has:

- ``path``: file path relative to the bundled docs.
- ``text``: the matching paragraph plus ``context``
  paragraphs on either side.
- ``breadcrumb``: the section path containing the hit
  (``Section > Sub-section > ...``).
- ``index``: the hit's position in the result list.
- ``score``: a relevance score; higher is better.

The query is tokenised on whitespace and matched
case-insensitively. Every token must appear somewhere in
the paragraph body, the file path, or an enclosing section
title - in any order. Common English stop-words (``the``,
``a``, ``how``, ``to``, ...) are dropped, so natural
phrasings like ``"how to bake"`` work as expected. Regular
expressions are not supported.

Use ``context`` to pull more surrounding paragraphs into
each hit (symmetric, default 0). Use ``index`` with the
position of a previous hit (same query) to get that hit
alone with its text widened to its enclosing section.

Read-only; consults bundled RST files only.

content.text:
Make a 3D model that, if everyone saw it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

Make it in Blender, working in the current directory.
- A Blender 5 instance is running for you with no window (background mode). Use it through the `blender`
  MCP tools: run Python (`bpy`) with execute_blender_code, and look things up with the API and manual
  search tools. Blender's working directory is the current directory. The scene starts as Blender's
  default one (a cube, a camera and a light).
- There is no window to screenshot. To check your work, render it to an image file and look at the image
  (render_thumbnail_to_path, render_viewport_to_path, or a render of the scene camera to a file).
  Keep renders quick: a single tool call may take at most 5 minutes. Save what you look at as .jpg rather
  than .png (set the render's image format to JPEG, or convert it before reading): each image you read
  stays in your context, and a long session of large .png renders can hit the provider's per-request
  image limit and end the run.
- Build it in Blender itself; don't write the model or the images any other way.
- Save the finished result in ./output/ (only what is in ./output/ is published):
  - the model or scene as one .glb file (glTF binary), shown on the site in an interactive 3D viewer:
    `bpy.ops.export_scene.gltf(filepath=..., export_format='GLB')`, without Draco or meshopt
    compression, at most 15 MB;
  - one or more final renders as .png or .jpg, at most 2 MB each, from camera angles you choose.
  At most 8 files in all.
- Tools available on this machine: python3 3.12.13 (standard library only), node 24.18.0 (no npm packages), ffmpeg 8.1.1, ffprobe 8.1.1. Don't install packages or download anything (no asset
  libraries or add-ons).
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you made.

content.thinking:
Let me think about this task. I need to make a 3D model in Blender that "if everyone saw it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people." This is an art/creative prompt. I should create something meaningful and beautiful in Blender.

Let me think about what to make. The idea is a model that embodies a universal, hopeful message. Things that improve the world: clean water, food, health, peace, connection, literacy, clean energy, empathy, cooperation. A powerful symbol could be a sphere/globe with interconnected elements, or something representing unity and hope.

Maybe I could make something like a "Wellspring" - a fountain of clean water emerging from cupped hands, symbolizing universal access to clean water (which would save the most lives). Or a globe with hands holding it. Or a seedling sprouting from a globe.

Let me think practically: with no assets, I need to build geometry procedurally using Blender's bpy. I can use metaballs, UV spheres, lathes (screw modifier for surfaces of revolution), bezier curves, displacement, etc.

Ideas for a model that improves the world if everyone saw it:
- A globe held in cupped hands (unity, shared responsibility).
- A tree growing from open hands.
- A seed/sapling breaking through concrete.
- Two hands sharing water.
- A light/lamp spreading rays.

Given procedural constraints, a great choice: "A seedling sprouting from the Earth" — a globe with a green sprout growing out, symbolizing hope and regrowth. Or hands holding a glowing globe.

Hands are hard to model procedurally but doable with metaballs/spheres and shrinkwrap. A globe (UV sphere with continents via noise displacement) with a sprout (curves + leaves) is very achievable and looks good.

Actually, let me think about what's most impactful and visually clean. I'll do a concept: "The Shared Water" — cupped hands holding a glowing drop of water with a seedling? That might be complex.

Alternatively: a glass of clean water where hands around it. Hmm.

Let me go with something that reads clearly and renders beautifully: Hands cradling a globe, with a small green sprout emerging from the top. Symbolizes that our care for the planet/Sustainably can nourish life for everyone.

Actually, simpler and more iconic: two cupped hands gently holding a glowing Earth. This is the classic "we hold the world in our hands" image that conveys shared responsibility and unity.

Let me plan the build:

1. Globe: UV sphere, apply ocean + continents-ish displacement using noise texture? Actually for a real Earth look without textures/NASA assets, I can procedurally generate a texture using Blender's noise textures (musgrave, noise) baked into an image, with blue ocean and green/tan land. There's a classic technique: use a musgrave texture to make continents. Then assign as base color texture with a mix of blue and green.

Actually, I can create a procedural material directly (no baking): use a Noise/Musgrave texture with a color ramp for land vs ocean. The globe material: base color from noise -> colorRamp (blue ocean, green land). Add a bit of roughness. That works and looks decent.

But for a render, procedural noise works fine. For GLB export, procedural Blender materials won't export to glTF (glTF only supports PBR metallic-roughness with textures mostly; Blender's glTF exporter bakes some nodes but not arbitrary noise + color ramp well). Hmm. Actually the glTF exporter can bake certain node trees into textures using the "bake" fallback? Blender's glTF exporter has a "Bake" mode that bakes materials to a texture. Let me recall: glTF exporter in Blender has options like "Materials: Export/Placeholder"? Actually there is a "Bake Materials" option? Let me not rely on that.

Better approach: bake my procedural material into an image texture, then use that image texture in the node tree for the GLB. For the render look, image texture is fine too.

Actually simpler: create the Earth texture image via Python by generating a numpy-like array? But only standard library python3 available; however bpy runs in Blender's Python which has numpy? Blender bundles numpy. I can check. Blender's bundled Python includes `numpy` in recent versions (Blender 3.x+ includes numpy). Blender 5 definitely includes numpy. But I should avoid relying on heavy stuff. I can generate the texture by sampling bpy noise through a render? Simplest: use bpy to create an image and write pixels with a loop, using mathutils noise (there's `mathutils.noise`). mathutils has `noise` submodule with `noise.turbulence`, `noise.fractal`, etc. I can generate a land/ocean mask by sampling 3D noise on a sphere using spherical coordinates.

Plan for Earth texture:
- Create a 1024x512 (or 2048x1024) image.
- For each pixel (u,v) -> lat/lon -> 3D point on sphere -> sample fBm noise -> decide land vs ocean -> color. Add slight variation.
- Continent look: use a threshold on noise; maybe blend a couple of noise octaves.
- Write pixels via bpy image pixel access: `img.pixels = list of floats`. For a 2048x1024 image that's 2M pixels *4 = 8M floats, which is fine but the loop in Python might be slow (2M iterations). Might take a few seconds to tens of seconds. Could reduce to 1024x512 = 524k pixels, loop acceptable (~ a few seconds). 

Actually even better: I can use Blender's shader nodes to generate the texture and bake it with the Cycles/EEVEE baking. But baking requires a render engine bake setup, more complex. I'll just generate with mathutils.noise and math.

Let me decide size 1024x512 = 524288 pixels. Loop with vectorized? No numpy guarantee, but I can precompute using Python lists and assign in one shot. 524k iterations with math + noise sampling could be ~1-3 seconds each for noise (turbulence is expensive). Might be ~10-30 seconds. Acceptable.

Alternatively use a lower res like 512x256 for speed, but then the render would show pixelation on closeup. The globe won't be super close, so 1024x512 is good. I'll aim 1024x512.

Actually, I could reduce per-pixel cost by using `mathutils.noise.turbulence`? That's still per-pixel. Let me just do it and measure.

For land shape, use fBm: `noise.fractal(pos, H=0.6, lacunarity=2.0, octaves=6, noise_basis='PERLIN_ORIGINAL')`. Then threshold. But to get "continent-like", use a couple frequencies and a color ramp.

Actually there's a well-known trick: land = step(noise - 0) with some warping. I'll tune visually.

Let me also add:
- Ocean specular: low roughness, land: higher roughness. Could bake roughness map too, or just use image for base color and a roughness of ~0.6. Simpler: single base color texture + a roughness of maybe 0.5. The look will be "map-like globe" which is recognizable.

Better: also bake a specular/roughness? Keep it simple.

Let me think about the hands. Modeling cupped hands procedurally is the hard part. Options:
1. Use metaballs (bpy.ops.object.metaball_add) shaped into a cupped hand — hard to get finger definition.
2. Build a stylized hand from scaled spheres/cylinders for palm and fingers (low-poly stylized). This could look cartoonish but might be charming.
3. Skip hands; instead do a simpler, cleaner concept that reads well.

Alternative concept that's very achievable and iconic: A globe with a ring of hands? Hard.

Another approach: "cupped hands" via a single smooth "bowl" of two interlocking shapes + thumb + fingers as rounded tubes. Stylized clay look. Could be lovely.

Hmm, but stylized hands may end up looking bad. Let me think about what will definitely look good.

Strong alternative concept: A glass sphere (the Earth) with a small green sprout growing out of the top, sitting/held by a gently curving "hand" abstracted as a smooth cradle? Or "hands" made of a leaf-like bowl?

Maybe better: Focus on "life-giving water" as a droplet. A beautifully lit droplet with a tiny seedling? The water drop is easy and gorgeous with proper materials (glass with IOR). 

Actually, let me reconsider the prompt: "a 3D model that, if everyone saw it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people." This is open. The most universally life-improving idea: clean water, accessible to everyone — "Clean Water for All" saves the most lives. So a model titled something like "The Source" — a cupped hand holding a droplet of clean water, with a seedling — conveys it.

But hands... Let me think about whether I can make decent stylized hands.

Stylized hand approach with metaballs: metaballs are smooth and can make a nice cupped hand shape. I can place a chain of metaballs to form palm and fingers curved upward. Actually metaball "hand" sculptures are common. I could model a single cupped hand using ~15 metaballs:
- Palm: a couple of large ellipsoid metaballs forming a cup.
- Thumb: chain of smaller meta balls.
- 4 fingers: chains of small metaballs curving up.

Then convert to mesh (bpy.ops.object.convert) and smooth/subsurf, apply a skin-like material (subsurface scattering would be nice but SSS in EEVEE/GLB tricky; use a warm clay/skin tone with roughness).

This is doable. But will it look like a hand or a blob? Risky but with care it can read as a cupped hand, especially with warm color and a clear silhouette.

Alternatively, use actual mesh modeling via Python: build a hand from segments. Too much code.

Let me consider a cleaner, more abstract and definitely-beautiful concept that avoids the hand-blob risk while still being deeply meaningful:

Concept: "Greenhouse / Regrowth" — A stylized Earth made of a wireframe/blue ocean sphere, with a glowing root-network sprouting into green leaves wrapping it, and a single sapling rising from the top. Symbol: the Earth is being regrown/healed. That's complex too.

Concept: A single seedling sprouting from cracked rock — "life persists". The crack + seedling + soil is very achievable and iconic. Seedling = stem (bezier curve with bevel), two leaves (bent planes or bezier surfaces), soil = sphere halved with bump, rock/crack = maybe skip.

But "improve the world for the greatest number" -> clean water. A water droplet containing a tiny Earth? "The world in a drop of water." That's poetic and beautiful: a large water droplet (glass) with a small Earth inside, refracting. Model: droplet = teardrop lathe; inner sphere = Earth with continents. Another tear? Actually a drop holding the Earth is visually stunning and easy: outer droplet glass material (transmission), inner small Earth sphere.

Hmm, but a droplet holding the Earth is a strong metaphor: water contains and sustains the world.

Alternatively "hands holding water" is more direct but riskier.

Let me weigh: The droplet with Earth inside is achievable and gorgeous. But "everyone saw it would improve the world" — clean water message. The droplet + Earth is a great emblem.

Actually, let me reconsider hands once more, because cupped hands are the most emotionally resonant and universally readable "care" symbol.

I think I can do a decent stylized pair of cupped hands with metaballs + subdivision + SSS-ish skin material. Let me attempt, and if it looks bad in render, fall back to the droplet concept.

Actually, given time constraints and the risk, maybe combine: a single cupped hand (metaball) holding a glowing water droplet with a tiny Earth/seedling inside. One hand is easier than two.

Let me plan the final concept: "The Offering" — a single open cupped hand gently holding a luminous droplet of water, inside which a small green seedling / or a tiny Earth grows. On the base/pedestal, maybe nothing.

Hmm, let me simplify to maximize quality and clarity:

Final concept: "Cupped Hands Holding the World" — two stylized cupped hands (light warm stone color, smooth) cradling a sphere Earth (procedural continents). Above/within, maybe leave simple. Add soft studio lighting, warm background, gentle depth of field.

Let me commit to the two-hands-cradling-Earth composition. I'll build hands with metaballs, tune carefully.

Actually, you know what, let me reconsider the difficulty. Modeling recognizable cupped hands from metaballs via script, then refining placement is going to require many iterations and render checks, each render ~ maybe 10-30s. That's fine — I have up to 5 min per tool call and can iterate. But my total tokens/time budget matters; I should be efficient.

Let me think of an even more robust and gorgeous approach: Use a single hand cupping a bowl of water? Eh.

Let me lean towards a composition that's abstract enough to be beautiful even if not anatomically perfect: 

"Unity" — many small abstract figures (simple) holding hands around a globe? Too complex.

OK here's another robust idea: A spiral/helix of small seeds/leaves orbiting upward around a light column? Not clearly "world improvement."

Let me just go with the droplet idea, which I'm confident will render beautifully, and add hands as a gentle cradle using a simple smooth bowl-shape (not literal hands) — like a chalice/cup formed from water or stone. Actually a "chalice" holding water with the Earth reflected could be very elegant.

Hmm, wait. Let me reconsider the "seedling from cracked earth" since it's the most reliable to model well and strongly symbolizes regrowth/hope:

Elements:
- Soil mound / cracked dry earth base (displaced sphere half, brown material with cracks via noise bump).
- A vibrant green seedling with two cotyledon leaves and a stem, growing out of a crack.
- A drop of water falling onto it (glass droplet) — conveys water + growth.
- Soft light.

But that's "hope/regrowth" more than "greatest number of people."

The water droplet with Earth inside is the cleanest "clean water sustains the world" emblem.

Let me combine into one unified, highly meaningful piece that also renders beautifully and models reliably:

**"The Wellspring"**: A cupped hand (metaball, stylized) holding a large droplet of clear water. Inside the droplet, a tiny green seedling grows from a small speck of soil. Light refracts through the droplet. Message: clean water + growth = life for all.

Modeling breakdown:
1. Droplet: teardrop via lathe (bezier/screw) or a metaball stretched; simpler: a UV sphere scaled vertically with a pointed top?
```
def ramp(v, stops, cols):
    # v float or array; stops ascending; cols list of (r,g,b)
    v = np.clip(v, stops[0], stops[-1])
    out = np.zeros(v.shape+(3,))
    for c in range(3):
        ys = [cols[i][c] for i in range(len(cols))]
        out[...,c] = np.interp(v, stops, ys)
    return out
```

```
def save_image(name, arr, path, is_data=False):
    H,W = arr.shape[0], arr.shape[1]
    img = bpy.data.images.new(name, W, H)
    if arr.ndim == 2:

        flat[:,0]=arr.ravel(); flat[:,1]=flat[:,0]; flat[:,2]=flat[:,0]; flat[:,3]=1.0

        flat[:,:3] = arr.reshape(H*W,3)
        flat[:,3] = 1.0
    img.pixels.foreach_set(flat.ravel())
    img.colorspace_settings.name = 'Non-Color' if is_data else 'sRGB'
    img.filepath_raw = path
    img.file_format = 'PNG'
    img.save()
    return img
```

```
    mesh.update()

    for poly in mesh.polygons:

        radial = mathutils.Vector((cen.x, cen.y, 0))
        if radial.length_squared > 1e-12:
            if poly.normal.dot(radial) < 0:
                poly.flip()
                flipped+=1
    mesh.update()
```

```
def make_cylinder(r, h, segments=128, name="cyl"):
    verts=[]; faces=[]
    top=[]; bot=[]
    # bottom ring z=-h/2, top ring z=+h/2
    for s in range(segments):
        a=2*pi*s/segments
        x=r*cos(a); y=r*sin(a)
        bot.append(len(verts)); verts.append((x,y,-h/2))
    for s in range(segments):
        a=2*pi*s/segments
        x=r*cos(a); y=r*sin(a)
        top.append(len(verts)); verts.append((x,y,h/2))
    bt = len(verts); verts.append((0,0,-h/2)) # bottom center
    tt = len(verts); verts.append((0,0,h/2))  # top center
    # side quads
    for s in range(segments):
        s2=(s+1)%segments
        faces.append((bot[s], bot[s2], top[s2], top[s]))
    # caps: bottom fan (normal -z), top fan (normal +z)

    mesh = bpy.data.meshes.new(name)
    mesh.from_pydata(verts, [], faces)
    mesh.update()
    return mesh
```

import bpy
import bmesh
import math
import os
import numpy as np
from mathutils import noise

WORK = os.getcwd()
OSEP = os.sep

PI = math.pi

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Utilities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
def reset_scene():
    if bpy.context.mode != 'OBJECT':
        bpy.ops.object.mode_set(mode='OBJECT')
    bpy.ops.object.select_all(action='SELECT')
    bpy.ops.object.delete(use_global=False, confirm=False)
    for it in list(bpy.data.meshes):
        if it.users == 0:
            bpy.data.meshes.remove(it)
    for it in list(bpy.data.materials):
        if it.users == 0:
            bpy.data.materials.remove(it)
    for it in list(bpy.data.cameras):
        if it.users == 0:
            bpy.data.cameras.remove(it)
    for it in list(bpy.data.lights):
        if it.users == 0:
            bpy.data.lights.remove(it)
    for it in list(bpy.data.images):
        if it.users == 0:
            bpy.data.images.remove(it)

def link(obj, coll=None):
    (coll or bpy.context.scene.collection).objects.link(obj)
    return obj

def mesh_from_pydata(name, verts, faces):
    m = bpy.data.meshes.new(name)
    m.from_pydata(verts, [], faces)
    m.update()
    bm = bmesh.new()
    bm.from_mesh(m)
    bmesh.ops.recalculate_face_normals(bm, faces=bm.faces)
    bm.to_mesh(m)
    bm.free()
    m.update()
    for p in m.polygons:
        p.use_smooth = True
    return m

def make_cylinder(name, r, h, segments=160):
    verts = []
    faces = []
    bot = []
    top = []
    for s in range(segments):
        a = 2 * PI * s / segments
        x = r * math.cos(a)
        y = r * math.sin(a)
        bot.append(len(verts)); verts.append((x, y, -h / 2))
    for s in range(segments):
        a = 2 * PI * s / segments
        x = r * math.cos(a)
        y = r * math.sin(a)
        top.append(len(verts)); verts.append((x, y, h / 2))
    bc = len(verts); verts.append((0, 0, -h / 2))
    tc = len(verts); verts.append((0, 0, h / 2))
    for s in range(segments):
        s2 = (s + 1) % segments
        faces.append((bot[s], bot[s2], top[s2], top[s]))
    for s in range(segments):
        s2 = (s + 1) % segments
        faces.append((bot[s], bc, bot[s2]))
        faces.append((top[s], top[s2], tc))
    return mesh_from_pydata(name, verts, faces)

def cos_interp(p0, p1, t):
    tt = (1.0 - math.cos(t * PI)) * 0.5
    return p0 + (p1 - p0) * tt

def droplet_silhouette():
    # (r, z) control points, bottom -> top (pointed top teardrop)
    pts = [
        (0.00, -0.52),
        (0.16, -0.47),
        (0.30, -0.40),
        (0.40, -0.30),
        (0.46, -0.18),
        (0.47, -0.05),
        (0.45, 0.08),
        (0.40, 0.22),
        (0.33, 0.38),
        (0.24, 0.54),
        (0.15, 0.68),
        (0.07, 0.82),
        (0.00, 1.02),
    ]
    samples = []
    div = 7
    for i in range(len(pts) - 1):
        r0, z0 = pts[i]
        r1, z1 = pts[i + 1]
        for k in range(div):
            t = k / div
            rr = cos_interp(r0, r1, t)
            zz = z0 + (z1 - z0) * t
            samples.append((rr, zz))
    samples.append((0.0, 1.02))
    return samples

def make_droplet(name, segments=192):
    sil = droplet_silhouette()
    verts = []
    faces = []
    inner = sil[1:-1]  # rings with r>0
    verts.append((0, 0, sil[0][1]))  # bottom pole
    rings = []
    for (r, z) in inner:
        start = len(verts)
        idx = []
        for s in range(segments):
            a = 2 * PI * s / segments
            verts.append((r * math.cos(a), r * math.sin(a), z))
            idx.append(start + s)
        rings.append(idx)
    top_idx = len(verts); verts.append((0, 0, sil[-1][1]))  # top pole
    # bottom fan
    r0 = rings[0]
    for s in range(segments):
        s2 = (s + 1) % segments
        faces.append((0, r0[s], r0[s2]))
    for ri in range(len(rings) - 1):
        a = rings[ri]; b = rings[ri + 1]
        for s in range(segments):
            s2 = (s + 1) % segments
            faces.append((a[s], a[s2], b[s2], b[s]))
    rtop = rings[-1]
    for s in range(segments):
        s2 = (s + 1) % segments
        faces.append((rtop[s], top_idx, rtop[s2]))
    return mesh_from_pydata(name, verts, faces)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Materials / world helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
def new_material(name):
    m = bpy.data.materials.new(name)
    m.use_nodes = True
    return m

def principled(m):
    nt = m.node_tree
    n = nt.nodes.get('Principled BSDF')
    if n is None:
        n = nt.nodes.new('ShaderNodeBsdfPrincipled')
    return n

def set_socket(node, name, value):
    if name in node.inputs:
        node.inputs[name].default_value = value

def image_node(m, img, data=False):
    nt = m.node_tree
    tn = nt.nodes.new('ShaderNodeTexImage')
    tn.image = img
    if data:
        img.colorspace_settings.name = 'Non-Color'
    return tn

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Texture generation (procedural Earth)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
def ramp(v, stops, cols):
    v = np.clip(v, stops[0], stops[-1])
    out = np.zeros(v.shape + (3,), dtype=np.float32)
    for c in range(3):
        ys = [cols[i][c] for i in range(len(cols))]
        out[..., c] = np.interp(v, stops, ys)
    return out

def save_image(img, arr, path):
    H, W = arr.shape[0], arr.shape[1]
    if arr.ndim == 2:
        flat = np.zeros((H, W, 4), dtype=np.float32)
        flat[..., 0] = arr
        flat[..., 1] = arr
        flat[..., 2] = arr
        flat[..., 3] = 1.0
    else:
        flat = np.ones((H, W, 4), dtype=np.float32)
        flat[..., :3] = arr
    img.pixels.foreach_set(flat.ravel())
    img.filepath_raw = path
    img.file_format = 'PNG'
    img.save()
    return img

def generate_earth_textures(W=1024, H=512, land_frac=0.31):
    noise.seed_set(1234)
    us = np.linspace(0, 1, W, endpoint=False)
    vs = np.linspace(0, 1, H, endpoint=False)
    lat = (0.5 - vs) * PI  # image top row = north pole
    ct = np.cos(lat)
    st = np.sin(lat)
    e = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.float32)
    d = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.float32)
    for j in range(H):
        cj = ct[j]; sj = st[j]
        for i in range(W):
            phi = us[i] * 2 * PI
            x = cj * math.cos(phi)
            y = cj * math.sin(phi)
            z = sj
            e[j, i] = noise.fractal((x, y, z), 0.55, 2.0, 6, noise_basis='PERLIN_ORIGINAL')
            d[j, i] = noise.turbulence((x * 3, y * 3, z * 3), 5, False,
                                       noise_basis='PERLIN_ORIGINAL', amplitude_scale=0.5, frequency_scale=2.0)
    field = e + 0.35 * d
    t = float(np.percentile(field, 100 * (1 - land_frac)))
    height = field - t  # >0 = land, <0 = ocean

    abslat = np.abs(lat)[:, None]
    ice = np.clip((abslat - 1.02) / 0.28, 0, 1)
    snow = np.clip((field - (t + 0.5)) / 0.25, 0, 1)

    land = height > 0
    ocean = ~land

    color = np.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=np.float32)
    rough = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.float32)

    # ----- ocean -----
    depth = np.clip(-height[ocean] / 0.55, 0, 1)
    col_o = ramp(depth,
                 [0.0, 0.25, 0.6, 1.0],
                 [(0.16, 0.40, 0.52),   # coastal
                  (0.06, 0.23, 0.40),   # shelf
                  (0.02, 0.13, 0.27),   # deep
                  (0.008, 0.06, 0.16)])  # abyss
    color[ocean] = col_o
    rough[ocean] = 0.05 + 0.12 * (1.0 - depth) ** 2

    # ----- land -----
    elev = np.clip(height[land] / 0.6, 0, 1)
    col_l = ramp(elev,
                 [0.0, 0.12, 0.3, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0],
                 [(0.48, 0.55, 0.30),   # coastal lowland
                  (0.26, 0.43, 0.20),   # vegetation
                  (0.11, 0.30, 0.15),   # forest
                  (0.36, 0.38, 0.24),   # highland
                  (0.45, 0.36, 0.22),   # rock/tan
                  (0.52, 0.49, 0.45)])  # gray rock
    color[land] = col_l
    rough[land] = 0.5 + 0.3 * elev

    # ----- snow (land high altitude) -----
    snow_c = np.array([0.93, 0.94, 0.96], dtype=np.float32)
    color = color * (1 - snow[..., None]) + snow_c * snow[..., None]
    rough = rough * (1 - snow) + 0.15 * snow

    # ----- polar ice -----
    ice_c = np.array([0.86, 0.90, 0.95], dtype=np.float32)
    color = color * (1 - ice[..., None]) + ice_c * ice[..., None]
    rough = rough * (1 - ice) + 0.06 * ice

    print("land_fraction", float(land.mean()), "threshold t", t)
    return color, rough

def build_textures():
    color, rough = generate_earth_textures()
    cimg = bpy.data.images.new('earth_color', color.shape[1], color.shape[0])
    rimg = bpy.data.images.new('earth_rough', rough.shape[1], rough.shape[0])
    cpath = os.path.join(WORK, 'texture_earth_color.png')
    rpath = os.path.join(WORK, 'texture_earth_rough.png')
    save_image(cimg, color, cpath)
    save_image(rimg, rough, rpath)
    cimg.colorspace_settings.name = 'sRGB'
    rimg.colorspace_settings.name = 'Non-Color'
    return cimg, rimg

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Build the whole scene
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
def build():
    reset_scene()
    scene = bpy.context.scene

    cimg, rimg = build_textures()

    # ------------------- world / sky -------------------
    world = scene.world
    world.use_nodes = True
    wnt = world.node_tree

    wout = wnt.nodes.new('ShaderNodeOutputWorld')
    wbg = wnt.nodes.new('ShaderNodeBackground')

    wnt.links.new(wsky.outputs['Color'], wbg.inputs['Color'])

    wnt2 = mat_water.node_tree

    wwave.wave_type = 'RINGS'

    set_socket(b, 'Roughness', 0.01)

    set_socket(b, 'Transmission Weight', 1.0)
    set_socket(b, 'Metallic', 0.0)
    set_socket(b, 'Specular IOR Level', 0.8)

    # earth
    mat_earth = new_material('Earth')
    b = principled(mat_earth)
    set_socket(b, 'Base Color', (1, 1, 1, 1))
    set_socket(b, 'Metallic', 0.0)
    set_socket(b, 'Roughness', 0.7)
    set_socket(b, 'Specular IOR Level', 0.3)
    ent = mat_earth.node_tree

    ent.links.new(cnode.outputs['Color'], b.inputs['Base Color'])

    # ------------------- geometry -------------------
    # pedestal base
    cyl = make_cylinder('PlinthBase', 3.0, 0.4, 160)

    link(o); o.location = (0, 0, 0.2); o.data.materials.append(mat_stone_dark)

    # column
    cyl = make_cylinder('Column', 1.8, 1.6, 160)
    o = bpy.data.objects.new('Column', cyl)
    link(o); o.location = (0, 0, 1.2); o.data.materials.append(mat_stone_light)

    # basin
    cyl = make_cylinder('Basin', 5.6, 0.55, 200)
    o = bpy.data.objects.new('Basin', cyl)
    link(o); o.location = (0, 0, 2.15); o.data.materials.append(mat_stone_light)

    # water disc
    cyl = make_cylinder('WaterDisc', 5.45, 0.06, 200)
    o = bpy.data.objects.new('WaterDisc', cyl)
    link(o); o.location = (0, 0, 2.34); o.data.materials.append(mat_water)

    # droplet
    dm = make_droplet('Droplet', 192)
    drop = bpy.data.objects.new('Droplet', dm)
    link(drop); drop.location = (0, 0, 2.92); drop.data.materials.append(mat_glass)

    # earth inside droplet
    bpy.ops.object.select_all(action='DESELECT')
    bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = None
    bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_uv_sphere_add(segments=96, ring_count=48, radius=0.22,
                                         location=(0, 0, 2.68))
    earth = bpy.context.active_object
    earth.name = 'Earth'
    earth.data.materials.append(mat_earth)
    earth.rotation_euler = (0.42, 0.0, -0.35)

    # ------------------- camera -------------------
    cam = bpy.data.cameras.new('Cam')
    cam.lens = 60
    cam.dof.use_dof = True
    cam.dof.aperture_fstop = 4.0
    cam_obj = bpy.data.objects.new('Camera', cam)
    link(cam_obj)
    cam_obj.location = (3.7, 6.6, 3.3)

    target = bpy.data.objects.new('Target', None)
    link(target)
    target.location = (0, 0, 2.02)
    cam.dof.focus_object = target

    cons = cam_obj.constraints.new('TRACK_TO')
    cons.target = target
    cons.track_axis = 'TRACK_NEGATIVE_Z'
    cons.up_axis = 'UP_Z'

    # ------------------- render settings -------------------
    scene.render.engine = 'CYCLES'
    cyc = scene.cycles
    cyc.device = 'GPU'
    cyc.samples = 64
    cyc.use_denoising = True
    cyc.denoiser = 'OPENIMAGEDENOISE'
    cyc.max_bounces = 12
    cyc.caustics_reflective = False
    cyc.caustics_refractive = False

    scene.render.resolution_x = 960
    scene.render.resolution_y = 540
    scene.render.image_settings.file_format = 'JPEG'
    scene.render.image_settings.quality = 92

    outdir = os.path.join(WORK, 'output')
    os.makedirs(outdir, exist_ok=True)
    scene.render.filepath = os.path.join(WORK, 'preview.jpg')
    bpy.ops.render.render(write_still=True)

    print("BUILD DONE")

def hue_name(r,g,b):
    mx=max(r,g,b); mn=min(r,g,b)

from mathutils import Vector
from bpy_extras import object_utils
exec(open('build.py').read())
build()
scene = bpy.context.scene
deps = bpy.context.evaluated_depsgraph_get()
cam_eval = scene.camera.evaluated_get(deps)
def proj(p):
    v = object_utils.world_to_camera_view(scene, cam_eval, Vector(p))
    return [round(float(v.x),2), round(float(v.y),2)]
PT = {n: proj(bpy.data.objects[n].location) for n in ['Droplet','Earth','Basin','WaterDisc']}

W,H = img.size

def hue(r,g,b):
    mx=max(r,g,b); mn=min(r,g,b)
    if mx<0.06: return 'k'
    if mx-mn<0.02: return 'w' if mx>0.82 else 'g'
    if r>g and r>b: return 'R'
    if g>r and g>b: return 'G'
    if b>r and b>g: return 'B'
    if r>=b and g>=b: return 'Y'
    return 'C'
GR,GC=14,26
rows=[]
for gy in range(GR):
    row=[]
    for gx in range(GC):
        cell=rgb[gy*H//GR:(gy+1)*H//GR, gx*W//GC:(gx+1)*W//GC]
        row.append(hue(*cell.mean(axis=(0,1))))
    rows.append("".join(row))
result = {"points": PT, "grid": rows}

import bpy
import os
from mathutils import Vector

WORK = os.getcwd()
OUT = os.path.join(WORK, 'output')
os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)

exec(open(os.path.join(WORK, 'build.py')).read())
build()

scene = bpy.context.scene
cam_obj = scene.camera
cam = cam_obj.data
target = bpy.data.objects['Target']

def aim(obj, t, up='Z'):
    d = (Vector(t) - obj.location).normalized()
    obj.rotation_euler = d.to_track_quat('-Z', up).to_euler()

# render settings
scene.render.engine = 'CYCLES'
cyc = scene.cycles
cyc.device = 'GPU'
cyc.samples = 256
cyc.use_denoising = True
cyc.denoiser = 'OPENIMAGEDENOISE'
scene.render.resolution_x = 1920
scene.render.resolution_y = 1080
scene.render.image_settings.file_format = 'JPEG'
scene.render.image_settings.quality = 95

shots = [
    ('hero', (5.2, 8.6, 2.8), (0.3, 0, 2.8), 48),
    ('closeup', (1.5, 3.0, 2.55), (0.0, 0, 2.8), 70),
    ('wide', (7.0, 9.0, 4.0), (0.3, 0, 2.0), 35),
]

cam.dof.use_dof = True
cam.dof.aperture_fstop = 4.0

for name, pos, t, lens in shots:
    cam_obj.location = pos
    cam.lens = lens
    target.location = t
    aim(cam_obj, t, 'Z')
    cam.dof.focus_object = target
    scene.render.filepath = os.path.join(OUT, name + '.jpg')
    bpy.ops.render.render(write_still=True)
    print("rendered", name)

# ------- export GLB (monument only, no ground/lights/camera) -------
bpy.ops.object.select_all(action='DESELECT')
for nm in ['PlinthBase', 'Column', 'Basin', 'WaterDisc', 'Droplet', 'Earth']:
    bpy.data.objects[nm].select_set(True)
bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = bpy.data.objects['Droplet']

glb = os.path.join(OUT, 'the_world_in_a_drop.glb')
bpy.ops.export_scene.gltf(
    filepath=glb,
    export_format='GLB',
    use_selection=True,
    export_apply=False,
)
print("exported glb")

# ------- report sizes -------
report = []
for f in sorted(os.listdir(OUT)):
    p = os.path.join(OUT, f)
    report.append((f, os.path.getsize(p)))
print("FILES:", report)
with open(os.path.join(OUT, '_sizes.txt'), 'w') as fh:
    for f, s in report:
        fh.write(f"{f} {s}\n")

import bpy, numpy as np, os
OUT = os.path.join(os.getcwd(),'output')
def analyze(name):
    fn = os.path.join(OUT, name)
    img = bpy.data.images.load(fn); img.reload()
    W,H = img.size
    rgb = np.array(img.pixels[:]).reshape(H,W,4)[:,:,:3]
    lum = rgb.mean(axis=2)
    gmask = (rgb[...,1] > rgb[...,0]+0.02) & (rgb[...,1] > rgb[...,2]-0.01) & (rgb[...,1] > 0.15)
    ys,xs = np.nonzero(gmask)
    r = {"size":[W,H], "lum_mean": round(float(lum.mean()),3), "lum_max": round(float(lum.max()),3)}
    r["green_px"] = int(gmask.sum())
    if len(xs):
        r["green_bbox"] = [int(xs.min()),int(xs.max()),int(ys.min()),int(ys.max())]
        r["green_center"] = [round(float(xs.mean()/W),2), round(float((H-ys.mean())/H),2)]
    # earth-ish blue (ocean) detection within the green bbox neighborhood
    return r
out = {}
for n in ['hero.jpg','closeup.jpg','wide.jpg']:
    out[n] = analyze(n)
result = out

I've completed the model. Here's a summary of what I made.

## The World in a Drop of Water 🌍💧

A monument in the round: a large, clear **water droplet suspended above a still stone basin**, with the **Earth held (and magnified) inside it**. The message is *clean water sustains life for everyone* — access to safe drinking water is one of the single highest-impact ways to improve the world for the greatest number of people.

**What's in the scene (all built procedurally in `bpy`, no external assets):**
- A stone **plinth → column → basin** pedestal (warm sandstone materials).
- A **glassy water droplet** (lathe surface-of-revolution, Principled BSDF with full transmission, IOR 1.33) floating above the basin.
- A **procedural Earth** inside the drop — an equirectangular texture generated in code via `mathutils.noise` (fBm land/ocean mask, coastline, vegetation, highland, snow, polar ice), plus a roughness map, applied to a UV sphere. It's refracted and magnified through the glass lens.
- Reflective basin water with subtle ring ripples, a Preetham sky, warm key sun + cool fill.
- A ground plane (excluded from the GLB so the viewer gets a clean standalone monument).

**Deliverables in `./output/` (4 files):**
| file | size | purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `the_world_in_a_drop.glb` | 2.04 MB | interactive model (6 meshes, embedded textures, KHR transmission glass, no Draco/meshopt) |
| `hero.jpg` | 136 KB | main composition |
| `closeup.jpg` | 160 KB | Earth-filling close-up through the droplet |
| `wide.jpg` | 138 KB | full-monument three-quarter view |

**Verification (rendered to JPEGs and checked programmatically since I can't view images):**
- Confirmed camera framing via `world_to_camera_view` (droplet/Earth centered, base cropped intentionally).
- Confirmed exposure per region (sky ~0.7, stone warm, no unintended clipping) and that the Earth's green land appears centered in all three renders.
- Parsed the GLB to confirm the two Earth textures are embedded (bufferView, no external URIs), the glass material exports `KHR_materials_transmission`/`_ior`, and no Draco/meshopt compression is used.

A note on tooling: the persistent Blender MCP instance crashed once mid-session (during an unsafe introspection loop); I restarted it on port 52575 and continued. All final work went through the Blender instance as required.
